description: AI & Software Engineering student in Tokyo building practical, data-driven solutions for Space Apps 2026. Experienced in Python, FastAPI, ML/ETL pipelines, Computer Vision, and 3D web visualization (JS/Three.js). Looking for motivated teammates in frontend, UI/UX design, data analysis, or space research to build a working prototype and a strong pitch. Languages: EN / JP / RU. Let's build something awesome!
summary:
We built NASA SEXTANT 3D & xEMU AR HUD to connect Mars route planning with what an astronaut actually sees inside their helmet during an EVA in Jezero Crater (18.38°N, 77.58°E). Using Python, FastAPI, NumPy, and Three.js, it combines an orbital 3D mission planner and a first-person suit visor into one continuous scene.

On a flat map, walking straight across Mars looks quick, yet it often leads crew over steep cliffs or into loose sand. Our SEXTANT A* solver blends MOLA elevation (-2545 m, g = 3.721 m/s²), HiRISE slopes, Odyssey THEMIS sand friction, CRISM/Perseverance targets like Cheyava Falls, and UHF radio range to plot safer paths that conserve O₂ (580 L tank). Switching to helmet view (1.8 m) gives astronauts live ECG vitals, a 20 m radar, a 220 m rock scanner, a forward Ingenuity drone (+14 dB relay), and ARIA-9, our onboard AI for rockfalls, leaks, dust devils, and solar storm evacuations.

Because Earth is too far for real-time radio help, giving crews autonomous 3D navigation and emergency support in English, Japanese, and Russian helps keep Mars surface missions safer.
details:
What our project does and how it works

If you look at Jezero Crater on a flat 2D map, walking in a straight line looks like the fastest way to reach a science target. On Mars, that straight line walks an astronaut straight off a steep cliff or into loose sand that drains their oxygen tank before they make it back. We built NASA SEXTANT 3D & xEMU AR HUD to connect pre-mission route planning with what an astronaut actually sees inside their helmet during an EVA.

The app runs in a browser as one continuous 3D scene around Jezero Crater (18.38°N, 77.58°E, MOLA baseline -2545 m, Mars gravity 3.721 m/s²). A Python backend computes terrain, radio signal shadows, and suit physiology on a 128 × 128 grid (10 m per cell across a 1280 × 1280 m zone), while Three.js renders an extended 3400 m procedural Neon-Mars horizon at 60 FPS.

In Phase 1 (Orbital Planning), you can flip between 5 NASA-modeled data layers: MOLA elevation, HiRISE slopes (<9° safe, >19° hazard cliffs), Odyssey THEMIS sand traps, CRISM/Perseverance mineral zones, and UHF radio line-of-sight from a 15 m tower at Olympus-1 Base. Our SEXTANT A* solver routes around steep grades (>21° blocked in normal mode) and deep sand, smoothing the path into an animated 3D ribbon. You can pick 3 preset traverses (EVA-01 to EVA-03), tweak safety sliders, or double-click right on the 3D ground to drop new waypoints. A side-by-side comparison mode drops crimson cones onto every steep cliff along a naive straight line and plots elevation against astronaut heart rate so you can visually see the oxygen and pulse difference.

In Phase 2 (Visor EVA), clicking Start EVA drops the camera smoothly down to 1.8 m helmet height with full 360° look controls. Inside the visor HUD you see a compass, real-time Canvas ECG trace (70–176 BPM), metabolic load (175–960 W), LCVG water cooling (18.0–27.8 °C), remaining oxygen from a 580 L tank, and a 20 m 8-sector proximity radar. You can also switch Mars lighting between Day, Sunset, and a Night LIDAR wireframe mode with a helmet spotlight.

Two teammates join the astronaut in the field:

• Ingenuity Scout Drone: flies 18 m ahead scanning terrain with a downward LIDAR cone, relays UHF signals (+14 dB boost) when canyon walls block the base, and has its own 360° orbit-and-zoom camera so you can inspect terrain around the crew.

• CRISM / PIXL Scanner & ARIA-9 AI: pointing the helmet reticle (or hitting auto-aim) within 220 m of 8 cataloged Jezero outcrops like Cheyava Falls (96% biosignature score) and Bright Angel (93%) pulls up 7 oxide bars and a 0.8–2.6 µm NIR curve. Meanwhile, ARIA-9 watches 180 m down the trail, answers crew questions, and handles 4 live emergencies we built in: [01] a rockfall blocking the path (drops a 42 m detour and replans A*), [02] a cooling fault and O₂ leak (26.4 °C / 162 BPM -> backup Loop B), [03] a 65 m dust devil (-28 dB signal drop -> drone relay + LIDAR), and [04] an SPE X9.4 solar storm that routes the crew immediately to the nearest shelter (Hephaestus Lava Tube 99.4%, Aurora Bunker 96.8%, Kodiak-South Alcove 92.0%, or Olympus-1 Base 99.8%).

Why it matters & expected impact

Mars EVAs cannot wait 4 to 20+ minutes for Earth Mission Control to spot a hazard over radio lag. Having orbital planning, drone reconnaissance, helmet biometrics, and autonomous emergency rerouting in one tool helps save critical suit oxygen, keep heart rates safe, and protect crews when weather or gear goes wrong. Since we built this for Tokyo Space Apps with an international team mindset, the entire app, AI assistant, and our 11-slide presentation switch cleanly between English, Japanese (日本語), and Russian.

Tools, languages & hardware we used

• Backend: Python 3, FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, Pydantic (4 REST API endpoints: /api/init, /api/route, /api/emergency-route, /api/probe).

• Frontend: Vanilla ES6 JavaScript, Three.js WebGL with OrbitControls, HTML5 Canvas 2D (ECG, radar, compass, spectrum, and elevation graphs), CSS3, and hand-crafted SVG aerospace icons, intentionally keeping zero heavy frameworks so it stays fast.

• Hardware: Developed and tested on standard laptops in regular desktop browsers so anyone can test it immediately without VR gear, though the HUD layout is structured to translate directly to WebXR visor headsets and real HiRISE GeoTIFF elevation tiles later.

What makes it creative & factors we considered

Our biggest design rule was to avoid building just another static 2D map dashboard. Connecting orbit view, drone recon, and helmet POV with a real camera dive and coupling terrain slope and sand straight to live ECG heart rate makes the physics easy to feel right away.

A few practical things we thought carefully about while building and testing:

1. Less noise inside the helmet: We initially added spoken AI voice readouts, then realized during testing that constant voice audio over alerts was distracting and felt intrusive, so we removed speech completely and kept ARIA-9 as a calm, compact visual ticker with a quick Q&A window.

2. Actually useful drone camera: A fixed drone chase camera felt limiting, so we upgraded it to full 360° drag rotation and scroll zoom to check blind ridges around the astronaut.

3. Uncluttered center vision: Important vitals sit on the edges of the visor while the middle stays open for terrain and rock scanning, plus one-click Night LIDAR mode when sunlight drops.
